speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the week end the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, Mr. Harold Wilson, advised me in advance of the special economic measures announced in Britain earlier today. The Minister of Finance received a supplementary message from Mr. Callaghan, the chancellor of the exchequer.
The British government, on the basis of a review of Britain's present financial and economic situation, particularly the current and prospective balance of payments deficit, has concluded that in addition to a number of internal measures designed to increase productivity and measures to encourage exports, immediate steps were necessary to reduce imports from all sources.
Accordingly the British government has decided to levy a temporary import charge of 15 per cent on imports other than-and the exceptions are very important for us- foodstuffs, basic raw materials, and unmanufactured tobacco. The exceptions, Mr. Speaker, are very important for us covering as they do a large proportion of our exports to the United Kingdom. No detail is as yet available as to the specific impact of this new charge on particular Canadian exports. However, it appears that in general it will apply to Canadian manufacturers. We are awaiting further information concerning the applicability of the charge to Canadian semimanufactured materials.
It is important to note that the new charge will apply to imports from all sources. Moreover, existing margins of tariff preference will not be altered. Mr. Wilson has told me how much he regrets that it has been necessary to impose charges on certain imports from the commonwealth, but Britain's nondiscriminatory obligations and the urgency of the situation left him no alternative. He has assured me that the new charges are essentially temporary and will be reduced as soon as the balance of payments situation 20220-5954
permits and abolished at the earliest opportunity. The British government will maintain the existing parity of sterling. Mr. Wilson has indicated that in this connection ample facilities are available for the support of sterling. Britain, Mr. Speaker, is Canada's second most important market and we value highly our trading relations with her. Britain's economic strength is important to Canada and to the rest of the world.
I have expressed our hope that the combination of measures introduced by Britain will result in the speedy restoration of balance of payments equilibrium and the earliest possible elimination of the special charge on imports. I have assured Mr. Wilson that he can count on the understanding of the Canadian government with respect to the present economic difficulties facing Britain and the necessity of measures on their part to overcome them.

subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING OTTAWA MEETING ON STAND-BY UNITS FOR PEACE FORCE

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING OTTAWA MEETING ON STAND-BY UNITS FOR PEACE FORCE
speechtext:
I wish to make a statement to the house on the peace keeping conference which will be held in Ottawa from November 2 to November 6. This meeting is the outcome of a suggestion made by the Prime Minister of Canada in his address before the general assembly of the United Nations on September 19, 1963. At that time the Prime Minister stated that Canada would welcome an opportunity to share its expe-

rience with other countries which have participated in United Nations peace keeping operations. To this end he proposed that there should be an examination by interested governments of the problems and techniques of these operations.
One of the main tasks confronting the United Nations is to find ways of strengthening and improving the peace keeping capacity of the organization, to learn from the experience gained in previous operations, and to seek more effective ways to perform this function in the future. The present meeting is a first step in that direction. As I explained to the standing committee on external affairs on July 9, the aim is to review past experience of the United Nations peace keeping operations and to exchange views on the practical and technical problems which have been encountered in the course of these operations. The meeting will provide an opportunity for informal discussions of these problems amongst the representatives of those countries which have made major contributions in men to United Nations peace keeping operations, or have formed stand-by units for possible service with the United Nations or announced their intention to do so.
Given the nature of the meeting, it is intended that representation should be at the working level and be drawn from persons mainly military experts, with practical knowledge of the problems. The exchange of views would be informal, confidential and without commitment. The points for discussion cover such questions affecting the work of United Nations peace keeping forces as composition; command; control and liaison; training and operational problems; environmental operating information; logistic support; personnel administration; public relations; accounting procedures and legal problems.
Members will note that all these are practical and technical problems, the kind that must be faced whenever a United Nations peace keeping force is organized. This is the first attempt to organize a meeting of this kind. Thus the meeting will be exploratory in nature, and the discussions will concentrate on the practical and technical problems involved in United Nations operations, with a view to strengthening the capability of the participating governments to serve and support the United Nations.
The wider political issues surrounding the authorization, control and financing of United Nations operations are to be discussed at the United Nations. This meeting will not deal
Ottawa Peace Keeping Conference with how future peace keeping operations are established or how they are financed. Nor will it attempt to set up a permanent United Nations force or to form co-ordinated stand-by arrangements. This is the responsibility of the United Nations itself.
We believe that the exchange of views will be fruitful and should be of great value to the participating governments. No formal steps will be taken to draw conclusions, and it will be for participating governments to decide what use to make of the information gained at the meeting.
We have already had informal assurances from the following governments that they are prepared to participate: Brazil, Colombia, Denmark, Finland, Ghana, India, Iran, Ireland, Italy, Malaysia, The Netherlands, Nigeria, Norway, Pakistan, Sweden, Tunisia, and the United Arab Republic. Formal invitations have been extended to these and other governments, and we are hopeful that a number of other countries will accept. The response thus far has been most encouraging.
I have instructed our ambassador at the United Stations to transmit the text of this statement to the secretary general of the United Nations this afternoon.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING OTTAWA MEETING ON STAND-BY UNITS FOR PEACE FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this meeting that is being convened will be most theoretical in its nature until some determination has been made as to the responsibilities of member nations within the United Nations to pay their shares and assessments of the costs of peace keeping.
This meeting is simply the formalization of what has taken place in the past among various peace keeping nations in informal discussions. Though it has been described as a significant step forward, in effect it is not of the consequence that some would give to it. Until there has been a settlement among the nations belonging to the United Nations, and a readiness by each nation to undertake its personal and several responsibilities as a member of that organization, meetings like this, while always helpful and always described as fruitful, will be meaningless.
I would like to hear the views of the Canadian government on the stand it will take in the United Nations regarding the U.S.S.R. and these other nations which, in a cavalier manner, have disregarded their pledged acceptance of the principles of the charter.
As for this conference, it will be a fine get-together, but I think it should be made clear that Canada and Canadians as a whole

Ottawa Peace Keeping Conference do not relish being in the position of playing their part in peace keeping while other nations, derelict in carrying out their responsibilities, do not assume that burden. That is the problem which should be faced. That is the problem which must be faced if the United Nations is to take effective action to ensure that peace keeping operations are maintained and that peace is preserved. This is simply window dressing until there is a decision made in the United Nations which will effectuate the principles of the charter.

subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING OTTAWA MEETING ON STAND-BY UNITS FOR PEACE FORCE
speechtext:
On behalf of this group I should like to welcome very warmly the announcement which has been made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Although there are serious problems, as the Leader of the Opposition has mentioned, from our point of view a conference of this sort is by no means meaningless. On the contrary, we think it has an important contribution to make.
If there is one feature of international affairs which has been a hopeful development it has been the gradual emergence and growth, step by step and from precedent to precedent, of peace keeping activities under the United Nations. We are fully conscious that these are only first steps and that there are many practical difficulties to be overcome. We believe Canada is in a unique position to make a contribution in this field, and we congratulate those responsible, including the government, for having this conference called in Canada. We wish the conference the very best of luck. We know this is only one step forward, but we believe it is an important tactical step and one which should be welcomed without reservation by the Canadian people.

subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING OTTAWA MEETING ON STAND-BY UNITS FOR PEACE FORCE
speechtext:
I am
sure we all agree that the principle of peace keeping is a most commendable one. On the other hand, when we consider the problems and issues which surround this important matter it becomes apparent that there is a great deal of misunderstanding and, I think, a good deal of regret that more substantial results do not accrue from the meetings which are held from time to time in this regard.
The minister has indicated that many of the most important policy problems will not be discussed at this conference, for instance the financing of peace keeping operations. Another matter which I believe should receive considerable attention is the finding of political solutions which would eliminate the causes


which necessitate the sending of peace keeping troops to these various areas.
As was pointed out, this is not necessarily a policy making conference; it is, rather, to be an information sharing conference. While it does not go as far as we would like, I believe it will be worth while and we wish the delegates success as they meet for these talks.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER TO EXAMINE PROPOSED RUN-THROUGHS
speechtext:
I should like to announce that the government has taken steps to appoint a commissioner to examine the proposals by Canadian National Railways for running through Nakina, Ontario, and Wainwright, Alberta, the matter discussed in this house on Friday. Following representations forwarded by the government on this matter to the president of the Canadian National Railways I was informed by telegram received from Mr. Gordon this morning that the company would be willing to withdraw run-through plans and withhold further action on their implementation pending an examination into the railways' proposals by an independent and impartial commissioner.
In reply to this telegram the government acknowledged the willingness of Canadian National Railways to withhold run-through plans and, conditional on this being done, is taking steps immediately to appoint a commissioner with appropriate terms of reference.
I wish, Mr. Speaker, to table copies in English and in French of the exchange of telegrams between Mr. Gordon and myself.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER TO EXAMINE PROPOSED RUN-THROUGHS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is too bad that this course was not followed before the matter became a crisis. I recall that it was brought before the house on several occasions and members in various parts of the opposition asked that action be taken. On October 22 I raised the matter, and again on the 23rd, in

order to find out the answer of the minister; whether he had transmitted the questions that had been asked to the president of Canadian National Railways and what the reply was. Now, when this sorry spectacle has developed into a serious situation-and the rail-waymen are not the ones responsible-this action is taken.
I find it difficult to understand the message from the president of Canadian National Railways to the Prime Minister in which he said:
We fully believe our discussions with employees affected and their union representatives would have reached amicable understandings as has been the case elsewhere and that present situation is due largely to intervention by third parties which has led to misunderstandings and distortions of actual situation.
I do not know who these third parties are, but on Friday last this house spoke with definiteness and clarity in this connection and demanded action. Now the action the government should have taken earlier is taken today. It is late, but at least it indicates that these third parties, members of parliament, when they express themselves for the Canadian people will be heard.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER TO EXAMINE PROPOSED RUN-THROUGHS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am tempted to move along the line of criticism of the Leader of the Opposition, but I forgo that temptation and raise a couple of points in connection with the Prime Minister's statement. The Prime Minister may be aware that there are at least 2,000 employees of Canadian National Railways all the way across the system from Montreal to Vancouver who are at present booked unfit for duty, or are sitting around the clock in union meetings.
I have received communications which indicate that while they are pleased the Prime Minister has taken this action, they would like at least two points cleared up. One is that there will be no recriminations and no disciplinary action contemplated by the management. There is nothing in the Prime Minister's statement or the wire from the president of the C.N.R. to touch on this. That is No. 1. The second is whether the terms of reference for the commission of inquiry will be general enough to take care of the points that should be considered.
I wanted to make this point clear. The three brotherhoods which have an interest in this matter, the engineers, the firemen and the trainmen, made representations to the Minister of Labour in connection with the statement of declaration of intent of Canadian National Railways to unilaterally operate crews through recognized terminals.
Appointment of Railway Commission
This was brought forward six months ago and is a request for just such a commission of inquiry, and it sets out the general terms of reference they would like. The first is to investigate unilateral actions of Canadian railways in changing working conditions and altering conditions of employment detrimental to the interests of their employees during the currency of a contract. The second-and this is the important part-is to study the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and the Railway Act to ascertain whether railway employees are adequately protected under existing legislation and interpretations relative thereto, and recommend any necessary amendments.
If these men are to go back to work it seems to me the government must go further, and go further immediately, with some information to the men, perhaps through management, that there will be no recriminations, and that the terms of reference will be broad enough so the inquiry is not just confined to the narrow situation in Nakina and Wainwright but that these other important considerations can also be taken care of.
I underline the importance of this because we do not get spontaneous reaction from Montreal to Vancouver, in respect of men scattered throughout the country, just on the basis of what has taken place at Nakina and Wainwright. I should like to ask the Prime Minister or the Minister of Labour whether they would take some action in respect of their comments so these men can get back to work and the C.N.R. can begin to move again. I should also like to ask that the documents be made an appendix to Hansard rather than merely tabled.

Mr. Speaker, all I have to say in this connection, related to what I said on Friday, is that we are very happy to have a commission set up to look into this matter, and that the management of the railways has decided not to proceed with the run-throughs, as a result of requests to delay their implementation.
In this connection, I believe the procedure now being followed will have good results. I must say that I have to agree with some of the remarks which have been made to the effect that we have not in the past taken this situation seriously enough, nor dealt with it as we should have done. I hope this same attitude will be taken in respect of other difficulties which may arise in future. The government should take action to prevent these difficulties from occurring, rather than

speechtext:
1.	Does Canadian Pacific Railways intend to reduce by 50 per cent its schedules in various regions of the province of Quebec and, among others, cancel the runs known as 202 and 203 between Lac Megantic and Montreal?
2.	Will the government ensure that no action will be taken until the population affected have been consulted?
3.	Will steps be taken by the government before October 25, 1964 to prevent or delay such reductions in service?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION IN C.P.R. SERVICE, QUEBEC
speechtext:
In respect of part 1, the board of transport commissioners advise as follows:
The following reductions in passenger train service have been announced by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to take effect on October 25, 1964:
Trains 202-203 which now operate daily between Montreal and Megantic, P.Q. are to be discontinued.
Trains 31-32 operating daily between Montreal and Farnham, P.Q. are to be discontinued. Trains 31-32 form part of a through service between Montreal and Boston.
Trains 137-138 now operating Saturday only and
Trains 132-133 now operating daily between Montreal and Ottawa via Lachute are to be discontinued.
The Canadian Pacific Railway Company has also indicated its intention to reduce the frequency of the passenger train service operating between Montreal and Mont Laurier, P.Q.
Notice of these changes was posted in all railway stations on the lines served by these trains on September 25, 1964. Concurrent with the posting of this notice, advice of the changes was also furnished the board.
Questions
Subsequently, the board directed the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to defer the effective date of these changes with respect to the Montreal-Farnham and Montreal-Ottawa services.
In the case of the Montreal-Farnham service, since this change would have involved a complete abandonment of passenger train service on a portion of this line in Canada, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has been advised that it will be necessary to secure the board's approval before making this change. Consequently, this reduction in service will not take place on October 25, 1964 as contemplated.
The change in service on the north shore line between Montreal and Ottawa represents a reduction in the existing service and as such does not require the board's prior approval. However, the substance of the submissions filed protesting this reduction in service caused the board to direct Canadian Pacific Railway Company to continue these trains pending consideration of these protests. The seriousness of the complaints received with respect to this particular service is such as to have prompted the board to set the matter down for public hearing.
A change is also being made in the Mont-real-Mont Laurier passenger train service effective on the same date. This change, however, does not involve the discontinuance of specific trains but a reduction in the frequency of their operation. Such a change in passenger train service does not require the board's approval.
Complaints have, however, reached the board with respect to this particular reduction as well as the proposed elimination of the local passenger train service between Montreal and Megantic. The board has directed the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to file its submissions with respect to the specific points raised in these complaints.
2 and 3. The Minister of Transport has no power to take such action but the steps taken by the board of transport commissioners are set out in the answer to part 1.

speechtext:

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

['Mr. Speaker, I cannot think of anything more important than interim supply. We will continue with the discussion of interim supply tomorrow. When it is concluded we will take up redistribution, and the labour code.']

We are dealing today, Mr. Chairman, with the third or fourth request by the government for interim supply. On this occasion it is for two months and this, of course, represents a very large amount of money. We should bear in mind, I think, that on the last occasion three months' supply was granted, and I feel it is incumbent upon members of this committee, especially in view of the fact that there is some doubt as to when the main estimates will come forward -from time to time additional items are brought in-to give this request close consideration.
If we consult a calendar we will find, if I recall correctly what a certain radio announcer said yesterday, that there are 66 or 67 days left before the end of the year. As far as this parliament is concerned it means possibly some 40 sitting days. The Minister of Fisheries, I believe, is doing some fast calculating; he is bringing in all kinds of things. If he wants to get down to a real discussion, then he and I can have one. I should like to get down to a worth-while discussion of the estimates of this government, including those of his department.
In these main estimates the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is responsible for some $88 million, and we are asked to approve one sixth of this amount on this occasion. But there is another item, to which reference may have been made at an earlier date in this house. At the back of the esti-

mates, among the money loans, is an item of $14J million to be lent to the corporation. Considering the type of operation carried on by the C.B.C. and the financing carried on by the corporation for a number of years, how is it expected that this loan will be repaid? The total budget of the corporation is far in excess of $88 million, in fact well over $100 million; the C.B.C. has certain revenues of its own. Yet the government of Canada is asked to make up a deficiency of some $88 million for the operation in the coming year. This sum of $14J million is presumably to meet expenditures of a capital nature.
In the past such expenditures have been included within the current budget, and when the corporation sought approval of parliament for the provision of the sums it needed, those capital requirements were included in the figure shown in the estimates; there was nothing tucked away in the back of the book. This is one question we should like to have answered. How is it expected that the corporation will repay this loan, and what will be the terms thereof? It behooves us to have more information that the Secretary of State, reporting for the corporation, has given today and on previous occasions when representations have been made from this side of the house and when, I am sure, they have been made by members on the government backbenches to the effect that it is high time the broadcasting committee was reconstituted to look into the affairs and policies of the corporation.
This is not with an idea of conducting a witch hunt. Mr. Chairman, I have to laugh at the sort of coy smile that appears on the face of the Minister of Fisheries when I say that because, after all, my connections with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are far in excess of his. For three years I was parliamentary secretary to the minister who reported to this house, and I had very cordial relations with the officers and know a good deal about the operations of the corporation. Certainly in the proposals that I make today I have no idea that this house should conduct a witch hunt; that parliament should become in any way a censor of the programming of the corporation, despite the pressures that are on members of parliament by their constituents, or out of their own desire, to bring some influence to bear on the programming standards of the corporation.
This is a public body, financed by public funds, and therefore has a responsibility per-
Interim Supply
haps even greater than a similar body with a private financial structure. It has been granted a tremendous responsibility by the Broadcasting Act, and I think in the main its record has been good. The officers of the corporation would be the first to admit that a review of their philosophies with regard to programming should be aired before the public, whereby they could place their views before a committee of members from all parties of this house. This would furnish them with the appropriate forum in which they could put across the philosophies of their programming and the principles of their operations. Then members of this house could more readily appreciate the problems and complexities of the operations of such a corporation. It is a big business. I cannot understand the hesitancy on the part of the government at this time, with the rather lame duck excuses made by the Secretary of State that the corporation could not or should not at this time be available for a complete review of its operations.
After all, Mr. Chairman, when hon. members who now occupy the treasury benches were sitting on this side of the house they were always after the government of the day to have the C.B.C. appear before a committee. As a matter of fact the broadcasting committee sat in 1959 and, if I recall correctly, it sat last in 1961. Three years have elapsed since that time; certain questions were under study then, and in a committee members could far better determine what progress has been made and what difficulties have been encountered in the formulation of future programming of the corporation and the extension of its services since 1961.
But no; we are told there is an advisory committee which will report in a confidential manner to the government. This advisory committee is headed by a man who had previously sat on a commission that had to do with broadcasting and who, frankly, made some recommendations that did not work out. This committee is to report to the government. Then, apparently under a cloak of confidentiality, policy will be determined and it will then be announced. It is said that then a broadcasting committee may be set up.
Just who is the government trying to fool? This is not going to help the corporation. It has a public relations responsibility to the viewing public, to the citizens of Canada; and I am afraid that at the present time its public relations have suffered, because never have we seen so much in print, either in letters to the editor, comments in newspaper

Interim, Supply
columns, or representations by members, about the nature of programming.
I readily agree that individual members should not be in the position of acting as censors, because what is one man's meat is another man's poison. But why this disquiet? It must mean that there is an uneasiness about the philosophy at the back of certain types of programs. Let us take the field of public affairs. I personally am very concerned as to why certain individuals seem to have a prominence on many programs; that they are the ones who are invited to be interviewed; that they are people who represent far-out ideas, whether they are from the right or from the left, whether they are of a wildly non-conformist view or whether they are just plain oddballs. It seems that the smart thing to do is to guarantee them a prime forum. They represent a minuscule of opinion in this country, and they could not buy the forum they are given.
Let us look at the situation at the time of the royal visit and after those unhappy events in Quebec city. What happened in the case of the leader of a very minor group, a man who had been castigated by the Prime Minister, by the Minister of Justice, by the premier of the province of Quebec, and by right thinking citizens across this country? The C.B.C. was indecently precipitate in putting him on one program called "Front Page Challenge". I am talking about the man Bourgault. Lo and behold, if that was not enough, on the Sunday night the Queen arrived in Ottawa I watched the program "This Hour has Seven Days" and one of the interviewers, with perhaps a touch of wry humour, indicated that the man who had done most to make the stay of the Queen in Quebec city unpleasant had not been able to appear on that Sunday program because he had been stopped, or he could not get to the studios because of the size of the crowds that were welcoming Her Majesty in Ottawa.
It is not that I object to the fact that a man is going to be interviewed on a program, but I do not understand why he should be allowed to use this forum. Last night the C.B.C. imported a man from the United States to Canada whose philosophy is that which was adopted by a group which many of us who served for years in Canadian armed forces, attempted to destroy. The hon. member for York South was mystified as to why he should be allowed or invited to appear.
Last year a man who had been convicted in the United States and fined thousands of

dollars, and was subject to further penalty in relation to downright dirty pornography, was brought to Canada for the purpose of interviewing him on a television program. I should like to know what is the philosophy behind this type of programming. These programs come into our living rooms, and as parents of children, who are very impressionable, we realize what detrimental effects this type of thing can have. It seems that the C.B.C. follows a policy in respect of programs whereby anything which is wrong, a deviation, or detracts from common decent morality or commonly accepted authority should be glorified.
The corporation does a great deal of good work in many fields. I hope to see it do much more work in the field of education. The C.B.C. does a great deal of good work in respect of its productions which show various areas of Canada to Canadians. It does good work in respect of its documentary productions, and in this regard it should be commended. On the other hand, are members of parliament asked to appear on C.B.C. programs to answer questions or present their views in respect of things that affect us all as Canadian citizens? That is not the case. Are members of parliament, or men in public life, asked to present their views in respect of certain films? That is not what is happening.
The thing I object to is the choice of individual who is interviewed on television. I do not know whether the officials of the C.B.C. are aware of this fact, but an individual who appears on television seems to have received a sort of seal of approval, or at least this is the impression in the minds of a great proportion of Canada's viewing public.
The hon. member for Grey North on several occasions has asked serious questions in respect of particular programs which have appeared as parts of series. Many of these programs have been highly objectionable because they are viewed by family groups. It is not sufficient to say that if we do not like or object to particular programs we should turn off the television set. That can be done, but some of the things which are shown and statements which are made are not foreseeable, and any harm that might be done will have been done before the set can be turned off. Many of these statements are made from one second to another, and one cannot avoid the possible harm by turning the set off after the objectionable things have been said.

I suggest we must receive answers to questions so that we will know why certain programs are being allowed. Many of them deal with subjects of morality. Not too many days ago on the program called "This Hour has Seven Days", individuals were interviewed about the contraceptive pill. The program contained street interviews of high school girls, and the view that these pills should be issued in high school was blithely presented. Apparently it was suggested that there is a lack of morality in our high schools, and because of human relationships these pills might just as well be made available. I wonder what could have been in the minds of the producers of this program when they allowed this expression of opinion by individuals interviewed on the streets, and what effect they think such an opinion would have on teenagers. While it may be of interest and benefit to discuss matters of this kind among adults, I can see no possible advantage in presenting this type of opinion to the people of Canada. Again I say that we must look into this situation and find out why the C.B.C. is allowing this type of program.
In this regard I should like to refer briefly to an article which appeared in today's Toronto Globe and Mail under the by-line of Dennis Braithwaite. The article is headed "Fighting Sin, C.B.C.". I do not intend to read this article, but wish to say that it is a protest by various groups against certain programs which seem to glorify sin, sexual deviation and crime. The people referred to in this article are not a group of oddballs, but are responsible citizens discharging their responsibility with respect to and concern with the things around them. The list of individuals includes members of fraternal organizations and women's organizations who are very concerned with this whole question.
During the past few years there has been a great deal of criticism in respect of the corporation because of its programming policy. Surely it is the duty of all members of this house who are charged with the safeguarding of the public interest to demand-and I do demand-an examination and a review of the C.B.C. There may be some point of view on the part of the corporation that we as individuals not connected with the broadcasting industry may not appreciate, and the corporation could put forward this view. I want to see this frank exchange of views in order to make what I think is a soundly based broadcasting organization function more efficiently.
I do not know whether the management of the corporation are deaf to the things that

are said by individual citizens in regard to what is done by the corporation. Certain producers, and what have you, move in rather arty circles where views are somewhat freer and there is perhaps not quite the same appreciation of everyday morality, but the fact is their views as to what should appear on television screens and come forth from loudspeakers do not necessarily represent what is the best for Canada.
I cannot share at all the views of the Secretary of State this afternoon that the management of a corporation could not possibly cope with committee hearings. They are much more able men than that. He is actually underestimating their capacity. In addition, it is not only the top management whom we would like to question. There is within the corporation a very extensive middle echelon and I think it would be most helpful to have these people explain their operations. It is not those who work at the headquarters of the C.B.C. and live in Ottawa who determine the exact nature of a program. After all, I am sure that the president and vice presidents only become aware of certain programs if they happen to see them on the screen and then it is too late to do anything about them.
Another aspect of the corporation that we would like to examine is its facilities. What are its plans for Vancouver? We have had a lot of questions on this matter. There is already a great deal of controversy between the city of Vancouver and the corporation. Let us help resolve the matter. Let us bring it out in the open where it can be examined and where the corporation can state its point of view.
What about Montreal? Where is the corporation heading there? What is being done? What progress is being made? In this regard it is not sufficient to have the minister responsible for the corporation answer questions on the discussion of his estimates. I am sure the estimates of his department and of the corporation will be among the last to be examined by the house and they will be caught in the gallop toward adjournment. This has happened so often in the past and it can easily happen again.
What about Toronto? There is an amount of $14 million here that we want explained. When we pass the motion for interim supply we will have granted eight twelfths or perhaps nine twelfths of the total amount of the estimates. This is more than the proper time to be discussing what the corporation is going to do.

I would refer to another point in which the hon. member for Churchill, the hon. member for Port Arthur and a number of hon. members from Newfoundland are also most interested. I have in mind the extension of services to outlying areas. It is three years since we have had a statement of policy in this regard informing us what the corporation planned to do at that time. We should like to know what it has done in the interval and what it intends to do in the future.
In the same vein, what about colour television? This will cost the Canadian people a vast sum of money not only for facilities for the C.B.C. but with regard to the private television network and also for individual receiving sets. This is a matter on which we must have some information from the corporation.
As an individual I should also like to see what the corporation is really doing with regard to planning in the field of educational programming and co-operation with the ministries of education of the provinces. We are interested in what can be done. What use is being made of visual instruction? I know it is already being done in a limited way in the schools for certain subjects at certain levels, but I think we should really look into this matter in view of the expected great shortage of teachers.
Yesterday I was talking to a man who had come to Ottawa for the Canadian universities conference. This year the universities have been hit with the front line of that wave of students who were born in the immediate post-war years, and the universities frankly do not know whether they are going to be able to cope with the problem. Is television part of the answer in order to deal with the shortage of teachers and the shortage of plant? I think we could get a worth-while contribution from the corporation in this regard by ascertaining what its ideas are on the subject. If it has no ideas we want to know why.
For these reasons I think the government has been most remiss in refusing to accede to the legitimate demands of members of the house for the setting up of the broadcasting committee many weeks ago. In my view

a lot of the difficulties and much of the criticism on orders of the day, which will continue, would have been taken care of if we could have had a broadcasting committee. I intend to emphasize this point again and again and I am sure my colleagues are going to do the same. I do not think it is the corporation that is at fault. Rather it is the government that is at fault by refusing to accede to our request for a parliamentary committee and prefering to set up its own little confidential advisory committee. I do not think that such a committee is a good answer to our requests.

Mr. Chairman, members of this party have been asking for a parliamentary committee on broadcasting for several months. There have been a number of reasons why we felt this was necessary and many of them were repeated once more by the hon. member for Edmonton West in his remarks. If the government, and the Secretary of State in particular, continue to refuse to set up this committee it leaves those of us who feel strongly about the matter with only one alternative, that is to take advantage of these interim supply motions from time to time to air our grievances about the operations of the C.B.C., thereby taking up a lot of time that could be devoted more properly to legislation. If this committee had been set up, all of these grievances and representations could be made in the committee. What is more, Mr. Chairman, this procedure would be more beneficial because we would have not only the senior officers but other officials from the C.B.C. before us and we could get some answers to the questions we ask.
Now, over the years, particularly during the last few months, whenever questions pertaining to programming or any other aspect of C.B.C. operations are posed to the Secretary of State, who has the responsibility of answering for the C.B.C. in this house, he consistently ducks the questions by saying, "I will communicate the opinion of my hon. friend to the C.B.C." He has also been fairly consistent, Mr. Chairman, in not coming back with the answers. As I have said, this leaves us no other course of action except continually to raise these grievances on interim supply motions. The hon. member for Edmonton West repeated something that has been said in this house on a number of occasions, that is that probably the estimates of the Secretary of State, which include the C.B.C. estimates, will be introduced during the dying hours of this session when there will be a rush to complete a number of tag

ends. We can look back over the record and find that last year the C.B.C. estimates were introduced after supper-it was after seven o'clock-on the last day of the session. I cannot but believe that this was done deliberately so that there could not be opportunity, or at least it would be awkward and inconvenient to have a detailed examination of some of the activities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
The year before that there was no detailed examination of the estimates of the C.B.C. This parliament, therefore, which is supposed to have some control of the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, has been completely denied any access to the officers of this corporation for the last three years. This parliament has been denied even the opportunity of interrogating the minister when the C.B.C. was asking for nearly $100 million of the taxpayers' money. We believe this practice has gone completely beyond reason. We do have a responsibility. So far as I am concerned, I am getting tired of providing the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation with a blank cheque for about $100 million every year without having the C.B.C. answer to this house for what they do with it, and whether or not the people who are providing that money are satisfied with the kind of service they are getting.
There is a great deal that could be said about the kind of programming in which the C.B.C. seems to persist, regardless of the protestations they receive. I can remember for example, there were protests in this house, and by way of letters to the newspapers all over the country, regarding a program called "Quest". I believe they even started a new season of "Quest" after these protestations were received, and the program continued for many months. The government never provided us with an opportunity to examine any officer or producer, whoever it is inside the organization, as to why they insisted on keeping this kind of program. I think that the whole moral structure of that which the C.B.C. is apparently prepared to present has deteriorated to such an extent that the members of this house have not only a right but an obligation to have a good, hard look at who is perpetuating this kind of thing.
It has been repeatedly stated, but I am going to say it again because we do not get any answers. The C.B.C. is responsible directly to parliament and to no one else. But we are in fact prevented from getting a minister involved in the details of answering for the activities of the Canadian Broadcast-
Interim Supply
ing Corporation. At the same time we are denied a parliamentary committee which would give us an opportunity to send for witnesses from this organization. Now, putting these two things together simply leaves you in a ridiculous, frustrated position. I believe it is about time the government took these protestations seriously. I am convinced that resentment amongst members of this house, and amongst Canadians generally, is building up to the point where some drastic action has to be taken and the people are prepared to support this kind of drastic action against the C.B.C.
It does not seem to me it is any protection for the members of the government to refuse parliament this broadcasting committee. I cannot understand why the government persists in its position. It is providing an internal examination conducted by another so-called committee. Perhaps this committee will perform a useful function, but why this should necessarily prevent the setting up of a parliamentary committee is beyond my comprehension. What is the government afraid of? What are the officers of the C.B.C. afraid of? If they are afraid of something, we ought to have them before us. As I have said, I am not concerned with whether or not it is convenient for the senior officers of the C.B.C. to meet a parliamentary committee. To me, this has no weight at all. I feel there has been enough representation that whether or not it is convenient for them they should be called and they should be prepared to testify to the kind of action they have been taking.
Now, Mr. Chairman, these protests have come from a number of parties in the house, and have come from a number of organizations. Perhaps in some respects you may say that this stems from some dissatisfaction with what the C.B.C. does about public affairs programs and how they allocate political time. Certainly there has been room for dispute about the justice of the manner in which they handle this, but it is considerably worse than that at this time.
The hon. member for Edmonton West referred briefly to an article in today's Globe and Mail, written by Dennis Braithwaite, and I should like to deal with it in more detail as it is pertinent to the matter before us this afternoon and is in line with the resentment building up in the country. I quote from the article as follows:
Did you ever hear of an all-Canadian movement called Declaration by Canadian Women? Its purpose, which it has been pursuing among women's organizations and church groups over the past year at least, is, in the words of its manifesto, "to end

Interim Supply
the domination of a minority who misuse the C.B.C. to spread propaganda for perversion, pornography, free love, blasphemy, dope, violence and crime." In its general preamble, attached to a petition form, Declaration states that both radio and t.v. are being exploited to maintain a constant assault on character, to undermine faith in God and respect for law and authority and to destroy sound home life and the knowledge of right and wrong. Noting that the C.B.C. last year spent $86 million of public money, the document calls on members of parliament to make the corporation "answerable to the Canadian people." Lest anyone think this is a demand for censorship, the declaration insists that the present freedom of the C.B.C. is a form of censorship. "Those who kill the conscience of a nation dig the grave of freedom and prepare the ground for dictatorship. It begins when God-given standards are mocked and their proponents are belittled, bullied, or silenced altogether."
This might be called a fairly strong statement, but let us have a look at those supporting Declaration by Canadian Women. They are people such as Mrs. Ward Markle of Toronto, president of the Ontario section of the Catholic women's league; Mrs. J. E. Houck, of Brampton, a former UN delegate and C.B.C. director; Senator Quart of Quebec; Ethel S. Wilson, minister without portfolio in the Alberta cabinet; Mrs. G. C. V. Hewson, president, Ontario division of the Canadian mental health association; Mrs. Cora R. Casselman, former member for parliament for Edmonton East; Mrs. A. D. Keith of Winnipeg, president of the women's Christian temperance union of Canada; Mrs. Isabel Ross, a member of the board of education of Toronto and Mrs. H. M. Schweitzer, past provincial commissioner of the girl guides of Saskatchewan.
The article adds:
While the language of the declaration can be dismissed as extremist and even hysterical, these names (there are 30 in all) carry weight. How did the usually circumspect C.B.C. manage to alienate so many of those who should be its friends and supporters?
The reason it has been able to alienate a lot of high placed and reasonable thinking people is its cavalier disregard of those protestations that were made during the past few months. We have come to the point where it is without doubt the responsibility of the government to set up this committee at once, first in order to clear up this matter of the protestations and second, to exonerate, if that is possible, a crown corporation that is financed from public funds to the extent of about $100 million a year.
We as members of parliament have no right to continue to provide public funds to an organization that has fallen into the

disrepute that the C.B.C. has. It is, as I said, incomprehensible to see the government adamantly refuse to shed some light on the reason officers of the C.B.C. are continuing to allow this kind of programming.
I believe the C.B.C. has probably done more to spotlight the divisions between English and French speaking Canadians than anything else, and has done so by giving repetitious attention to the extremist viewpoints. For the most part we in this parliament consider these divisions as one of the most serious problems facing the nation, yet when protestations are made through the Secretary of State to the C.B.C. to stop providing a platform for these extremist viewpoints, we are told we must not be concerned with C.B.C. programming.
Another thing which disturbs me is the tremendous expansion of the C.B.C. If it is responsible only to parliament I would like to know where it got the authority to continue to expand year after year to its present magnitude. I have never heard anyone on the floor of this house demanding that the C.B.C. expand its activities and its budget year after year, but when I say that I must make one modification. There has been a demand for the C.B.C. to extend its broadcasting facilities through satellites in order to carry its signals into some areas that are not served by any television channel. That is a valid request for expansion, but to my knowledge no member of parliament has requested that the C.B.C. continually expand its budget.
Over the past ten or 12 years the C.B.C.'s estimates have grown from $25 million to $50 million to $70 million and are now well over $100 million annually. In this connection I would point out that the argument advanced by the hon. member for Edmonton West, that its estimates for operations are a little deceptive, is a valid one. Prior to 1964-65 the C.B.C. has included in its estimates so much for operations and so much for capital works or the expansion of capital works. We all know very well that when it starts out on a $30 million or $40 million building in Toronto or Montreal, but only requests something like $10 million or $14 million in the first year, once we approve that initial expenditure we are hooked for the rest of it.
In addition to the matter of loans this is a complete deception because, as has been pointed out, the C.B.C. does not have any substantial income other than that voted by

parliament. So when it calls these moneys loans we know very well they will have to be paid back out of appropriations passed later by parliament. In my opinion this is not a proper way to proceed and present estimates. It is a kind of subterfuge to circumvent what may be required under the law respecting estimates, and it gives the C.B.C. the opportunity to spend more money than is indicated. These are some of the more important reasons we need the officers from the C.B.C. before us.
On a number of occasions we in this party have taken the position that there is neither a fair distribution of free political time nor objective reporting of the news from this parliament. We have seen a screen of silence come down within the C.B.C. over the activities of members of this party in the House of Commons, and we should like to have someone from the C.B.C. explain why this is being done. I know that members of the Social Credit party have been most vociferous in their criticism of the corporation. We do not apologize for that. What is more, we intend to continue this criticism in line with what we consider to be our responsibility. If this is some kind of revenge being practised on this party in the allocation of free political time and also in the imposition of a news blackout upon us, those concerned may as well know now that we do not intend to be intimidated by actions of this kind. I have asked the Secretary of State in this house at least three times to tell me how the C.B.C. allocates time to the various political parties on both the national and the provincial scene. The program on the national level is, I believe, called "The Nation's Business" and at provincial level it is called "Provincial Affairs", at least in Alberta.
I happen to know that in some years, 1961 and 1962 particularly, there was a difference of as much as 61 to one. Yet when the C.B.C. allocated time on "Provincial Affairs" in Alberta they gave the same time to the party with one member in the provincial legislature as they did to the party which had 61 members. I happen to know that one of the conditions they laid down before any time was granted on the national scene was that a party should have some members in the House of Commons. Yet there were occasions in Alberta in the "Provincial Affairs" program when free time was given to speakers belonging to a party which did not have a single member in the provincial legislature. My hon. friend from Cariboo tells me it is that way in British Columbia now.
Interim Supply
This is not fair, and we have asked time and again: who is it who sets down the formula? Who makes the decisions, and why are they not consistent as between one area and another or one province and the next? The Social Credit party to my knowledge has not been provided with any free time on "Provincial Affairs" broadcasts in any province where it has no elected members. Yet we find parties in Alberta and B.C., parties which have no members in the legislatures, being given time. Why? Who sets up the formula? Who decides these things? We never get answers from the Secretary of State or from his parliamentary secretary who replies from time to time. We want to get answers to these questions. We do not want to be dismissed with elusive remarks and perhaps a smile. To us this is a serious matter. We believe that when we are called upon to provide $100 million for a public broadcasting system and are told consistently that this corporation is responsible to parliament and to parliament alone, there should be some opportunity for the members of this parliament to interrogate the officers of the corporation. That ought to be clear. It does not seem to me that there is any ambiguity about that request. But still the government adamantly refuses to set up the committee to enable us to look into this question.
There are many other questions which should be asked. The committee should look into allegations concerning the management of news; allegations with respect to the type of individual who is asked to appear on public affairs programs. We should like to find out why certain patterns are followed. No one can deny that this forum which is provided by the C.B.C. does have a profound influence on public opinion in Canada. Certainly, if it does not, it is a complete failure because it is one of the major media of communication with the masses in Canada. So it seems to me that the government could save itself a lot of headache and a lot of time on interim supply motions if it would move quickly to set up this parliamentary committee on broadcasting and clear the air with regard to some of the allegations which have been made. Serious allegations made by very responsible people have not been dealt with.
Members of the opposition have been criticized for taking too much time in the House of Commons on supply motions and other matters. If the way in which the government has handled the queries which have come to it concerning the C.B.C. is to continue there will certainly be a lot more time taken up. I heard it said this afternoon that a lot of time

Interim Supply
could be saved in the question period preceding orders of the day if the government would agree to set up this committee, and I believe this to be a fact. Indeed as the days go by I am sure more questions will be asked before orders of the day are called, and a lot more time will be used to discuss matters on the floor of this house unless we are given an opportunity to examine some of the officers of the corporation.
I cannot understand why the government appears to be protecting the C.B.C. at the present time. Our examination of the officials need not interfere in any way with the work of this other committee, this secret committee or whatever you want to call it, which the government itself has set up. Even if we did not receive satisfactory answers from the officials of the C.B.C. to the extent that we could revise the relationship between the corporation and members of this house, at least we would have the opportunity to indicate to those officials the opinions coming to us from the people we represent. This process is the essence of democracy as far as I am concerned. Asking members of this house to provide money for a corporation while at the same time refusing them an opportunity to examine the affairs of that corporation is, to me, the exact opposite of democratic procedure. So I hope the government will understand that there is increasing pressure to establish this parliamentary committee, and the sooner they get on with it the sooner we will be able to have some time and clear up some of the business before the house.

I have but a few comments to make, Mr. Chairman. Further to the previous speaker's remarks, I would point out that members on this side of the house have no objection whatever to seeing those of the opposition do their duty.
I think many hon. members would benefit greatly by being a bit more concise in their remarks. Some of them go on until their time has run out, when they could easily cut down what they have to say to ten or 15 minutes. As for me, I should like to give evidence of such conciseness in the points I wish to make in this debate.
Last Friday during the debate on interim supply the house dealt with C.N.R. lines. Today we are discussing the C.B.C. For my part, I feel that the most important problem facing us now is that of national unity. That is why I should like to take the opportunity afforded me by the examination of interim supply to express a few ideas.

In my opinion, what is missing in our country at present is the development of a Canadian ideal. Regionalism is showing itself here and there across Canada. Often an excessive provincialism also manifests itself. I feel it would be much more in keeping with this desire to achieve the Canadian ideal to look after, if not the creation, at least the consolidation of a Canadian ideal.
What is a Canadian ideal? If it can be summed up schematically, it is an ideal according to which one believes in the expansion and dissemination of the two fundamental cultures of our country. Many speeches are heard on both sides. Speeches intended to proclaim equality of rights, speeches intended to illustrate the greatness and beauty of our two national cultures. However, on the practical level, tremendous deficiencies become evident.
This is why I feel it is urgent-and this becomes imperative for the federal government-to work unceasingly on this task, in order to create, to consolidate and to strengthen a Canadian ideal.
Today Canadians co-operate mainly for economic purposes. But we need more than solidarity on the economic level. I believe that we should all acquire a deep patriotic ideal, which at present does not exist.
As far as I am concerned, I would approve the federal government taking the initiative in this area, because if it is held in suspicion among French speaking Canadians, it is due to the fact that it was realized and it is still being realized that the federal government does not seem interested in promoting French culture. What the French Canadians obtain, they always gain after bitter demands, often after recriminations, and we are wondering if this complex of recrimination is not being forced into us; at times, this becomes an exhausting task.
In my opinion, the federal government must assume a determining initiative in the area of national unity. It could, for instance, create a department of French culture, as a division perhaps of the Secretary of State department. There is nothing contrary to this in our constitution. The emergency created today by the stormy events of the last several months certainly indicates a crisis in our national unity, and we know that according to our constitution, peace, order and good administration in Canada fall under the jurisdiction of the federal government. This department of French culture would not in any way violate any provision of our constitution, because the Massey-Levesque commission

established very fine shades, subtle distinctions between the area of education and that of primary and secondary education, which falls exclusively and which will always fall exclusively under the jurisdiction of the provinces; distinctions made between the field of education and that of culture as such.
That is why, in my opinion, it would be quite consistent with our constitution for the federal government to take the initiative in this area by creating a department of French culture and thereby take advantage of the new spirit in this regard. This must be pointed out, in order to pay tribute to those who show this fine attitude. Attention must be drawn to this new climate which prevails in a goodly part of the English speaking population, which today shows a far greater understanding of the French fact than it did some 25 or 30 years ago.
For my part, I must say that within the Liberal party-I do not wish to make a political issue of this, but I must say that I could not feel more at ease than I do within the Liberal party, and I feel that this spirit of mutual understanding, which is favourable to biculturalism, is due in the first place to the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Pearson.)
Mr. Chairman, while establishing a department of culture, we could refer to some figures which are most significant and promote the French culture from coast to coast, instead of limiting it to Quebec.
Statistics show that, in all provinces of the country, there is a French fact. It is more or less powerful, according to the demographic strength of the various provinces. So, may I point out to you that, in Prince Edward Island, 8.8 per cent of the population is French speaking, in Nova Scotia, 6.9 per cent is French speaking, in Manitoba, 8.2 per cent, in Alberta, the figure is lower, but still significant, 4.7 per cent. In British Columbia, 3.6 per cent. In Ontario, figures are a little more comforting, that is 9.4 per cent; in New Brunswick, 37.8 per cent of the population is French speaking.
What part would a department of French culture play? Its importance would be as follows:	I quoted figures relating to the
French speaking population in the various provinces; if one now refers to the people of French origin, one notes a set-back, because many people of French origin in certain provinces can no longer speak French. Therefore, a certain assimilation took place. I do not hesitate to say that the Durham report belongs to the past.
Interim Supply
There is no question today of assimilating the French speaking population. On the contrary, this new climate which should make us happy, instead of promoting this assimilation, tends more to encourage the development and the growth of the French fact.
Mr. Chairman, assimilation has been fairly intensive in all provinces. In Prince Edward Island, for instance, 16.6 per cent of the population is of French origin but only 8.8 per cent speak French. In Nova Scotia, 12 per cent of the people are of French origin but only 6.9 per cent of them are French speaking. In New Brunswick, 38.8 per cent of the population is of French origin but only 37.8 per cent speak French, there being a loss of 1 per cent in that province.
In the province of Ontario, 10.3 per cent of the people are of French origin but only 9.4 per cent of them are French speaking. Comparative figures for Manitoba are 9.1 and 8.2 per cent. The situation is the same in the other provinces.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, so as to put an end to this assimilation movement, to promote an atmosphere of national unity, to show that the great principles we advocate with regard to bilingualism and biculturalism do not remain meaningless and empty statements, I think it is time, now more than ever, for the federal government to stop being: suspected of furthering assimilation, since on the contrary the federal government must strive by all available means to keep these-two cultures, these two civilizations in our country more flourishing than ever.
I would add a suggestion, Mr. Chairman, in order to accomplish which seems to me the-most urgent task: There is a royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism whose terms of reference in my opinion, should be-extended to include a study of a vital and essential problem, i.e. immigration.
As we know, immigration is the chief instrument through which the French cause-could be served, for immigration can affect the population pattern in this country. At the-present time, immigration could be one of the greatest instruments at our disposal. I said it again and again, and repeat it once more today, immigration has always operated against the French fact.
I believe immigration is a vital problem* and the terms of reference of the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism should be broadened to include a study of' this serious problem, as it affects national-unity and the French fact, so that a fair

Interim Supply
balance might exist and that French Canada be no longer victimized by our immigration policy.
There is another instrument which can be beneficial to French Canada. I refer to television, which comes under the Secretary of State and to which there could be added another branch, that of French culture. Television could then play a leading part and be beneficial to us.
I believe that in promoting the French fact we shall create that climate of national unity which is becoming more and more essential at this juncture.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member who has just resumed his seat brought certain aspects of this debate to your attention and to the attention of this committee. I noticed particularly that he related his remarks to the actions of the C.B.C., the biculturalism and bilingualism commission, to immigration and to a new spirit of cooperation. He also suggested that a new minister be appointed in respect of the C.B.C. The hon. member also referred to contributions to French culture, and called attention to certain percentages.
At this time I do not mention these items by way of criticism, but should like to point out that in spite of the fact that on many occasions during past weeks, months and even years when these questions have been asked, the minister responsible to parliament for the operation of the C.B.C. has not been in his place. That is a significant fact which should be brought to the attention of this committee, and possibly to the attention of the public as a whole. I think the public should be made aware of the situation, in view of the fact that this crown corporation is asking us to approve, by passing these estimates an expenditure in the neighbourhood of $88 million. I should like to remind this committee that these are tax dollars, and we are only discussing a portion of them today. The hon. member for Edmonton West earlier today drew attention to capital loans in the amount of $14,500,000. To use the vernacular, Mr. Chairman, that ain't hay.
I have in my hand an article written by an individual closely associated with broadcasting, which relates directly to certain points I should like to refer to this afternoon. Basically this article dealing with broadcasting principles, particularly of the C.B.C., reads in part as follows:

In principle, it is parliament which determines the roles of the various elements within the Canadian broadcasting system. However, in practice-
I should like to repeat that for emphasis, Mr. Chairman.
However, in practice parliament has confined itself to the declaration of certain broad national objectives without offering many specific instructions concerning how the goals are to be achieved. For the most part, it is content to examine, and usually approve, methods devised by others.
For example, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has placed its own interpretation on its simply worded parliamentary mandate to provide "a national broadcasting service". The corporation has devised policies, which, in its judgment, meet this requirement and these it refers, periodically, to parliament for endorsation. Since the corporation's inception, this procedure has been a significant feature of its operations. It has been followed consistently, and without serious parliamentary criticism. Consequently, the C.B.C. is justified in assuming that it is interpreting its role correctly.
Mr. Chairman, after this quotation from a prominent broadcaster in respect of his interpretation of the C.B.C.'s role in the Canadian broadcasting system I should like to refer to specific cases, to which almost violent objection has been taken both in this and that other place, as a result of representations by Canadian citizens. I should like also to refer to specific statements which have been made both during the question period and during the debate in this committee this afternoon. I refer again to this sentence from the quotation: "It has been followed consistently, and without serious parliamentary criticism". This can hardly be so, Mr. Chairman. As the member for one constituency it would be my conclusion that in some cases the C.B.C. has almost flagrantly disregarded public opinion. As I pointed out earlier, almost violent representations have been made to members, and I will put some of them on the record later.
There is also a general misunderstanding among the Canadian public with regard to the very conception of a crown corporation. We as members of the house understand what is really meant when it is said that the C.B.C. or any other crown corporation is subject to parliamentary control. But there is general misunderstanding among the Canadian people with regard to the C.B.C. in particular and this may be because people are so much more familiar with the actions of this crown corporation. The average Canadian citizen or taxpayer has the impression that control of the C.B.C. by parliament may be obtained by a mere objection or prayer or petition to his representative in parliament. Few people realize that control by parliament actually means control by the government in

the first instance, second, by the House of Commons and, third, by the other place. Very few people indeed realize that there has to be a combination of expression of views by all three before the management of the crown corporation really listens to parliament.
We had a good example earlier today in connection with Canadian National Railways. How many times and for how long have objections been raised in the house with regard to the C.N.R. which as a crown corporation is in my view almost identical to the C.B.C.? For a long, long time in committee of the whole house we have heard objections about certain aspects of the management of the C.N.R. But what happened? Actually the situation was allowed to deteriorate to such an extent that the railway personnel had to take action which resulted in service to the people being curtailed.
When was the control finally exercised by parliament? Earlier today there was tabled in the house a communication between the Prime Minister and the head of the crown corporation. After years of representations and many complaints, only then did the crown corporation come close to being controlled by parliament and even then the control was temporary.
In my view the government, or at least the minister responsible for reporting to the house for the C.B.C., should take note of some of the things that have been said today. I have pointed out the final reaction with regard to complaints and disputes about one corporation, and in so far as the C.B.C. is concerned I hope that things do not have to proceed to that point in order to have the management of the C.B.C. at least listen to some of the complaints made in parliament, particularly by people who feel that such a crown corporation should be controlled by parliament. After all, the people who are elected to represent the taxpayers of Canada certainly should be listened to with regard to crown corporations more so than has been the case for some time past.
I mentioned earlier that revisions in C.B.C. programming have only been made in some cases, not all, after almost violent objections by decent, intelligent citizens. If I may, I should like to put something on the record in this regard. The letter to which I wish to refer has to do with a program no longer broadcast but it bears on the point we are talking about today. The letter is signed, is from Lethbridge and is dated February 26 of 20220-597
