this year. It is addressed to me as a member of parliament and reads as follows:
Dear Sir:
I am writing to you to complain about that program "Quest".
I know this is old hash but it does bear on the point I am trying to make this afternoon.
I think it is the most filthy program I have ever seen and last night it was terrible. Everybody around here is disgusted. It makes you ashamed to be a Canadian. It is no good writing to the C.B.C. They have had so many letters and pay no attention to it. I think it should be taken off the air. It is surely no program for teenagers. If you have not seen it, especially last night's, I wish you could.
I might interject that I did not see the program.
Usually we turn "Quest" off, but we left it on last night and it was disgusting. I can't understand the players. Don't they feel embarrassed playing parts in a thing like that? I thought I would write to you and see if there is anything you can do. Thanking you for your time...
P.S. There have been a lot of people here talking over telephone this morning and everybody is disgusted with last night's "Quest" program. The C.B.C. have quite a lot of good programs.
I want to emphasize that too, Mr. Chairman. The C.B.C. has a lot of good programs.
Why spoil it by putting on things like last night's?
That brings up another point, and may I say I do not mean to be completely critical, Mr. Chairman. Many Canadians, I among them, are very proud of the corporation, particularly because of the fact that service was made possible long ago to people who might not yet have either radio or television broadcasting service. The position of the corporation has been jealously guarded and I think it should continue to be. However, the corporation also has a primary responsibility in that it has a captive audience and therefore the corporation must give first place to its primary responsibility. In my view its primary responsibility encompasses such things as educational programs, factual programs, factual reporting of the news and so on.
The hon. member for Edmonton West brought forward a good point when he mentioned education by television. In the more remote areas, this applies to radio as well. I think we could go even further than that and refer to the impact that television and radio have today on the written word. I believe that the power of the written word is still the most powerful influence today. Not only do we have a responsibility in so far as television and radio are concerned, therefore, but television and radio have a respon-

Interim Supply
sibility today with regard to their influence on the press, as we commonly refer to the written word. This, to me, is very important.
In order to emphasize what I said earlier, I want to refer to a current happening. The Canadian people have the idea, with regard to the C.B.C. as well as other crown corporations, that this parliament shall determine the various roles of the various elements within the Canadian structure. I said in the beginning, and I want to repeat this, that if parliament is to control or even to consider the role the C.B.C. and other crown corporations have in the general Canadian structure, then why is the minister responsible for reporting to parliament on the C.B.C. absent when we are discussing this matter?
I will explain that in a moment.
Now?
No, as soon as the hon. member completes his remarks.

I hope it will be a good explanation and I appreciate hearing from the minister. Nevertheless this question will be a matter of record today. The hon. member who spoke before me mentioned some new ideas. They were good ideas. I agree with them, probably with the exception of his reference to a percentage of French and English. I am not talking about that, I am talking as a Canadian. I am thinking of Canada as a whole. I do not care about percentages here and there. Some of the best friends I have are probably members of smaller groups. Perhaps hon. members in the house at the moment belong to one of the larger groups but, Mr. Chairman, I have no idea whatever of referring to these percentages. I am talking about Canada as a whole and the benefits to be derived by Canada as a whole. If other hon. members want to refer to this topic in terms of percentages, then whatever I have to say I am quite sure will not have any bearing on these percentages.
Frankly, Mr. Chairman, I dislike hearing Canadians referred to in terms of percentages. I think Canadians are Canadians. I feel, too, that we have something of which we should be very proud. I feel that our constitution, the British North America Act, or however you want to refer to it, is something of which Canadians as a whole from one end of this country to the other can be very proud.
Say that to the member for Three Rivers.

I will say that to any member in this house. I am putting it on the record and I am quite sure it will be public. I say sincerely and honestly that we in this house, the members in the other place, and the people of Canada can be proud of our articles of confederation, the British North America Act, the constitution or whatever you want to call it. It is something of which we should not only be proud but something we should advertise. It might very well be, Mr. Chairman, that the C.B.C. could have done this a couple of weeks ago. We have something of which we can be proud and something to show the rest of the world. Sure, we have our troubles, and we have people right here talking about percentages. Surely we, as Canadians, we in this house, have something of which we can be very proud and we should advertise it to the whole world. The C.B.C. could well have done so some time ago and Canada's image throughout the world would be better than it is today.
I hope you will forgive me, Mr. Chairman, for getting sidetracked but I felt very sincerely that I had to say these things. I thank the hon. member opposite for reminding me of this because it was away down in my notes.
We did not want you to miss anything important.
How much more important could anything be? If you have a different version, I will gladly yield the floor to you.
You are right.

O.K., then; keep smiling and we will get through.
There is something else that I want to mention, and I referred to it a moment ago. I should like to refer to the Queen's visit. We have to realize that during this time the sovereign probably could have been humiliated to some extent. I am rather hesitant about bringing this matter forward, but I do feel that I must. I just said a moment ago that the C.B.C. might have done something along this line.
I note from a popular magazine and from the press that there were 400 reporters from the C.B.C. alone reporting the visit of Her Majesty to Quebec city, and I am reminded of the fact that many years ago, and under different circumstances, a club known as the 400 club was formed. I wonder if the C.B.C. is trying to form a new 400 club. There were 400

reporters there, but what did we see and what did we hear?
Did the hon. member say 400 reporters or 400 employees?
I said 400 newsmen-reporters.
I thought the hon. member meant employees.
No, I said reporters covering the event-reporters, cameramen. Perhaps I should have said employees-but 400 personnel were there.
Four hundred C.B.C. men?
Four hundred men, including cameramen, copymen-
Employees.
All right, employees. It is the same thing; 400 C.B.C. personnel.
Where?

At Quebec. If any hon. members opposite want to give their version I will yield the floor to them. Some of them may have other facts and if they want to put their version on the record I will let them. Does anybody deny that the C.B.C. had 400 personnel at the Quebec visit?
Not reporters.
I said personnel.
No, you said reporters.
Admittedly I said reporters, but quite frankly I meant personnel.
Why did you say reporters?
Because he meant personnel.
Were you there?
In Quebec, yes.

Mr. Chairman, I may have made a little mistake, but may I continue. Roughly there were 400 there. I am not going to say 399 or 400 or 401 because members opposite might get the facts and say there were 398 or 402 and I would be shown to be wrong; but generally speaking there were 400 personnel from the C.B.C. covering Her Majesty's Quebec visit. What did the Canadian public get from this?

speechtext: Is it agreed?
Agreed.
We like you.

Thank you very much. It is very seldom I get that sort of agreement. The point I want to make is that what we saw on t.v., heard on the radio and read in the press was not the actual facts of the case. I know the press will criticize what I have been saying today and will refer to one short program that showed us what actually took place. But generally speaking throughout the period of the visit what we were shown were empty streets, the lack of flags flying and that sort of thing. True enough there was one short program, I think it was on "News Magazine", that reported the visit fully, but surely we could have had more than that. Earlier I said something should have been done in the matter of public relations. There should have been programs dealing with confederation, the B.N.A. Act and the things of which Canada has reason to be proud. We did not see that; we did not hear it; we did not read it.
I want to thank hon. members for the extra time they have allowed me.

Mr. Chairman, I feel obliged to interject a few remarks at this point in the proceedings to remind the committee of one or two relevant facts as I see them, with which some members may not agree, but which I think should be drawn to the attention of the committee. Before doing so, however, I wish to answer a question asked by

Interim Supply
the hon. member for Lethbridge who has just resumed his seat. He asked why the minister responsible to the house for the C.B.C. was not here to discuss these estimates. The answer is very clear, that we are not now discussing the main estimates. We are merely discussing interim supply for the expenditure of moneys for a two month period.
The detailed estimates of departments are examined by the committee of the whole house and may be approved or rejected as the committee sees fit. That being the situation, it has not been the custom in this parliament to have the individual ministers come to the committee discussing interim supply to answer for their departments. Rather it has been the custom-
May I ask a question?

Yes, in just a moment. Rather, it has been the custom to discuss the details of the estimates when they are before the house and to discuss on interim supply any major grievance against the administration that the opposition parties may have. That is the reason why the individual ministers are not here to answer for their individual departments and for the details of the individual items involved in the main estimates.

Does the President of the Privy Council not recall the many instances when he and his colleagues were on this side and they used to try to castigate a former minister of finance on this particular point?

Yes, I recall that experience very well and I have based my remarks on it. I recall how careful the opposition of that day was to confine its attack on the then government, on one occasion for its failure to bring in a budget in a fiscal year, and on another occasion for certain matters having to do with the Bank of Canada. I recall very well how careful the opposition was, not to discuss the details of the main estimates on interim supply.
That is nonsense.

The hon. member is entitled to his opinion of my remarks. I might remind him that I did him the courtesy when he was speaking of not expressing my opinion of the remarks he was making earlier this afternoon. I thought that was the courteous procedure to follow in committee of the whole. I refrained from any comment while he was speaking. I
[Mr. Mcllraith.1
know he follows a different procedure but that is his privilege and his responsibility-
The hon. gentleman's halo hangs heavy.

In any event, I do wish to point out to the committee, and I believe it is my obligation to do so although some hon. members may differ from me on this, that we have now, in this session of parliament, had supply before the house on some 72 days out of a total of 176; that we have been calling estimates for consideration three days out of five every week, with one exception, for many weeks in the recent past, and that in the United Kingdom parliament the time allowed for supply is only some 26 days for the whole year, though I agree the procedure followed there differs from our procedure in Canada. If the government is devoting three days out of five to supply, surely on interim supply we should not be discussing details of the estimates of particular departments? I invite the committee to consider that notwithstanding the fact that some 70 full days debate on supply have taken place this year-I point out in all fairness that instead of taking the permitted 12 days on supply motions the opposition only required seven days out of 12 and generously gave up five days-notwithstanding the fact I have mentioned, we have only succeeded in approving the estimates of only eight departments out of some 26.
I would point out, also, that though today we have been discussing the affairs of the C.B.C. almost exclusively, no opposition group has requested that the estimates of the C.B.C. be called before the committee of the whole when we are considering main estimates. If the opposition wants to discuss these estimates they can be brought forward on a convenient day very soon and I invite members of this committee to consider whether we should not do better if we were to pass this interim supply bill now and devote the time we would otherwise spend on it, considering main estimates. If there are any suggestions which would expedite the final passage of the main estimates, which hon. members opposite in any of the groups or parties wish to make which would bring to a conclusion the examination of the estimates within a reasonable length of time, bearing in mind that we have already spent 70 days on supply this year, the government would be very willing to listen to such suggestions and consider them very carefully. I feel it is my obligation to bring this matter to the attention of hon. members because it must be readily apparent that in the light of the legislative program on

the order paper and with the approach of Christmas, having had no adjournment since the house started its work earlier this year, some thought should surely be given to the subject. I make this appeal to hon. members because it seems to me, having listened attentively and carefully to the debate this afternoon, that the whole of the discussion might better have taken place on the main estimates.
It was a different situation on Friday when hon. members felt they needed to raise a subject matter of urgent and special significance which could not wait until the main estimates were called. But we have three days on estimates this week and if hon. members have suggestions for additional days in the week, for calling and considering estimates I would be very glad to have their proposals considered by the government. I make an appeal to hon. members to consider this matter and, if they have any views on it, to bring them forward.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, after the remarks which have just been made by the President of the Privy Council I would not have proceeded with my observations had I not noticed that two or three other members were rising at the same time. Indeed, I find myself indulging in a sentence which opens many speeches in this house, namely, "I had not intended to take part in this debate, but-
However, it seems to me that even the devil deserves an advocate. The devil in question may not appreciate my being the advocate but I do feel something should be said in this day's debate on the other side of the issue, as far as the C.B.C. is concerned. The fact is that every speech on this subject this afternoon has been a speech in which the C.B.C. has been treated as a popular whipping boy. It is true the C.B.C. makes mistakes from time to time; it would probably go on making mistakes even were it to listen to the criticisms voiced in this house. But there are one or two things which might be said on the other side.
First of all, I want to congratulate the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on being the subject of controversy. If there were no controversy surrounding the C.B.C., if nobody complained about anything which appeared on the C.B.C. programs, it would not be worth five cents of public money. It is to the credit of the corporation that it is presenting challenging programs, that it is making us look at new ideas. It is to its credit that people are expressing their views pro and
Interim Supply
con about what appears on C.B.C. television programs or over its radio network. There are times when I myself am critical of some of the things I hear and see and, like other members of this house, I do not think the C.B.C. gives me proper coverage for my work in the House of Commons. But the C.B.C. is like the press in that respect. We are used to that.
You will get it, now.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
We shall just have to wait and see. Surely this is a time in man's history when it is necessary for us to do some new thinking. Some of the great organizations of our time are going through agonizing reappraisals of their thought, their doctrine and their position. This is of great importance both for them and for our society. I believe that to the extent the C.B.C. presents to us new ideas and makes us look at the problems of our country, of our hemisphere, of our world and, indeed, one might say today, of our universe, it is doing us a service.
This does not mean we are denied the right to be critical of some of the programs which are broadcast. However, I think there should also be an occasional word of commendation and I welcome this opportunity to voice that word at this moment. I doubt whether the argument over last night's program in which this fellow Rockwell appeared will ever be settled. There will be those who will contend as long as we recall it that it should not have been put on. There will be others who will think it was a good idea to put on this program. I shall not at this moment try to settle that argument one way or another, but since so much has been said against the Rockwell interview having been aired over television, may I suggest there could be some advantage from its having been broadcast? Surely the Canadian people now realize what racism can lead to; surely we have had a picture of how serious can be anti-Semitism, antipathy toward negroes, toward coloured races, toward people who disagree with us. Surely people can realize that Hitlerism, so far as its ideas are concerned, is not necessarily dead because world war II is over.
I fully appreciate the views of the Zionist organization of Canada and of the Royal Canadian Legion and others, who still wonder whether that program should have been aired last night-and it is a good question; but I suggest there is also the other side, and that maybe it has helped us in Canada to realize that we want no part of racism, of totalitarianism or of the kind of arrogance

Interim Supply
that was displayed by that man on our television screens last night. John Drainie's prediction, so far as I am concerned, was correct; I was shocked, sickened and disturbed by what I saw. But I dare to believe that Canadians generally will have been so shocked, sickened and disturbed that there will be an increasing opposition to any form of racism in this country.
There have been many appeals this afternoon to the government to set up a committee on broadcasting so that the C.B.C. can appear before that committee. I agree that there ought from time to time to be reviews of broadcasting policy. I think, indeed, that once in a while there has to be a review by a royal commission-not just by a private advisory committee such as we now have, but a full-dress royal commission. I also think that from time to time there has to be a review by a committee of parliament. This is the way you keep broadcasting by a public body responsible to parliament and, through parliament, responsible to the people. But in between these reviews I insist that the board of governors, the management of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, should be free to arrange its programming and should not be subject to censorship by the government; neither should it be subject to interference in its day to day programming by members of parliament. We are free to make our complaints; we are as free as any citizens of the country-but surely, having set up a corporation to do a job, having given it the policies we think it should carry on, we should give it the opportunity to carry on those policies. If we do not like them, if we disagree with the things that are being done, our function is to get rid of the board of governors, to get rid of the management and bring in new people to do the job.
It is very common in this house to talk about the way things are done in Britain. As members are probably aware, the activities of the B.B.C. are not even permitted to be the subject of the kind of questioning, in the House of Commons at Westminster, that goes on here in the House of Commons in Ottawa. There the attitude is taken that the B.B.C. is set up as an autonomous body, and in between the times its work is reviewed it is free to do what it thinks is the best job in broadcasting, subject to the knowledge that if it does not do a job that is satisfactory to the people, the management will be changed, the board will be fired. It seems to me that should be our approach, rather than the attitude of heckling at and carping

about the C.B.C. day in and day out, as goes on in this house.
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, that seems inconsistent with the opening remarks I offered when I congratulated the C.B.C. on being the subject of controversy. But if it is going to be attacked, not only in letters to the editors of our newspapers, not only in the columns our columnists write and in editorials, but also here on the floor of the House of Commons-and I take no objection to the criticism because I think it is good that members stand up and express their clear and honest views about what is happening-I suggest there is also a place for those of us on the other side, who feel that the C.B.C. is doing a good job, to say so in the course of a debate of this kind.
As I said earlier, Mr. Chairman, I think that the C.B.C., like any other organization run by human beings, has made many mistakes. Sometimes its public relations are rather poor. I think sometimes its advance announcements as to what is going to be broadcast have not been fully thought out. I believe, like anybody who advertises his products, the C.B.C. sometimes overemphasizes what is coming and the show it has not boosted turns out to be better than the show that has been boosted for a week or so. But in the main this organization is trying to help Canadians to think; it is trying to help us look at the problems which face this country; it is trying to bring to the radio and television audiences the things that are happening in this country; it is trying to give our artists, performers, speakers, and so on, the opportunity to put forward their views. I think that in the main the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is doing a good job. It deserves to be looked at critically; but it also deserves once in a while to be told that it is doing a good job.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Gladly.

The hon. member stated that the C.B.C. should be criticized when it abuses its licence, when it brings forth programs that deal with hatred; but I gathered from his remarks earlier that he did not think this criticism should come from members of parliament. Am I correct in believing that he feels they should be criticized by anyone but members of parliament?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Chairman, whether or not a program on C.B.C. is one

that deserves negative criticism is of course a matter of opinion. But if I did not make myself clear before, I thank the hon. member for Renfrew South for giving me this opportunity to make myself clear. I believe it is perfectly proper for members of parliament to voice their criticism in a debate such as this, provided we do not dictate to the C.B.C. what it should do; but my main point is that, with everybody else expressing negative criticism, I thought there should also be opportunity for someone to express positive criticism, and that is what I have tried to do.

Mr. Chairman, before the supper hour we were privileged to hear a few words from the minister, the hon. member for Ottawa West. It seemed to me that he was complaining that we were discussing the C.B.C. today because he thought that the details should be discussed at some other time. As I listened to the debate today it did not seem to me that we were discussing the details, but a broad outline of a policy under which the C.B.C. might be a more effective instrument on behalf of the Canadian public. It was very strange that the minister should change his mind so soon, because only on Friday a matter was referred to by the hon. member for Port Arthur and the hon. member for Melville, which the minister at that time thought did not deserve enough attention to set aside the normal business of the house, but that the details of that matter should be gone into during our consideration of interim supply.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the hon. member does not want to misrepresent me. The proceedings of Friday are on record, and he will find that what took place is quite different from what he is asserting, in so far as the record represents what I put forward. What I did suggest was that since there was an opportunity to discuss what was the major complaint of the opposition concerning the government on interim
Interim Supply
supply later in the afternoon it should proberly be discussed then, rather than on a special motion to adjourn the house.
The point I made today is that since we are discussing the C.B.C. estimates, the proper place to discuss them is during the consideration of the main estimates and not on interim supply. That statement was accompanied by my offer to have the main estimates brought forward, since we are already giving three days a week to a consideration of them.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has aptly defended my point, because the details of the C.B.C. have not been discussed. We have been discussing general policy. He has come to the defence of the position I have taken. I think the record of last Friday will indicate in no uncertain terms that that is the case. However, I do not intend to go into that phase of the discussion at all tonight, Mr. Chairman.
At this time we are being asked to vote $740 million for the carrying forward of the government's program for the next two months. Naturally the opposition must ask itself why it should vote this money. As I asked myself that question tonight I found it very difficult indeed to find any reason why the government opposite should be given $740 million necessary to carry on the business of this country for the next two months, and I make that statement because of the conditions which exist in this country today.
Mr. Chairman, one need only look back to last Friday and what happened at that time to realize that this government never moves until it is almost too late to consider problems which deserve attention. I think that fact is made clear by the action taken over the week end by the minister and the government, and indicates that the debate which took place last Friday could very well have been dispensed with had this government done its duty in regard to the particular matter under consideration at that time. I refer to the railway problem.
The problems affecting agriculture today, and I think immediately of the plight of the turkey growers of this country, and the government's lack of action, represent one reason for not voting confidence in the government, but for withholding supply. The decline in the price being paid for cattle across this country and the lack of action on the part of the government is another indication of why steps should be taken to withhold interim supply from the government opposite.

Oh, oh.

Interim Supply

I note there are some hon. members who represent the areas concerned, where there has been crop failure in eastern Canada and in parts of the province of Quebec, and I should like to ask you, sir, what this government is providing in this vote of $740 million for the relief of those people? One need only think of the dairy problems in eastern Canada today to ask what this government has done to alleviate that situation.
When we pick up our daily newspapers these days what do we see? We see an indication by this government opposite that there is to be a tax cut some time in the near future. This announcement is only a belated reparation of the damage done to the economy of the country by the Gordon budgets, which brought forward an 11 per cent sales tax which is stifling industry, to a certain extent, and reducing the full impact of increasing employment which could have been ours had the government followed the policy which should have been followed.
Oh, oh.

That is another indication of the carelessness of hon. members opposite. When one thinks of the $740 million required by the government to run the affairs of this country for two months, he at the same time can only think of inflation and the alarming increase in the cost of living which today is eroding the value of the Canadian dollar to consumers in every part of the country. When one thinks of the situation, bearing in mind the tremendous increase in consumer credit in this country today, he cannot but ask what action the government opposite is proposing to meet that situation? Mr. Chairman, my principal purpose is to speak for a few minutes on the subject of the C.B.C. Quite a number of speakers have dealt with it at some length today. They took up a considerable part of parliament's time to talk about it and I think I am justified in using a little of its time to speak on the same subject.
First, may I say we are always interested in hearing the monthly state of the union address by the hon. member for Rosthern, who tonight indicates that he sees danger signs to the Canadian economy. If we are to judge from recent newspaper reports probably the danger signs he sees are that the budget may be balanced this year after seven years of monumental deficits. In his state of the union address he omitted that, and failed to mention anything about the reestablishment of fiscal responsibility, about the buoyant economy, or about the reduction in unemployment.
However, referring to the C.B.C. the hon. member had a good idea when he said it was useful to review the early days of the corporation and its early purposes. Its principal purpose was that of uniting the nation and developing cultural interest in the country. I am in full accord with those principles. As I have said previously in this chamber, if it had not been for the existence of the C.B.C. in the early days of radio, and in the early days of television, it is doubtful whether Canadian culture could have been salvaged. Had it not been for the C.B.C. our culture could well have been submerged in American culture because of the great influx of U.S. television programs.
In passing, I wonder how many singers and artists have been discovered and encouraged over the years by the C.B.C. I wonder how many people across Canada have had their knowledge of public affairs broadened by the C.B.C. I wonder whether any broadcasting network in the world has kept a higher standard in news broadcasts than the C.B.C. No organization has done more to provide entertainment in the medium of sports coverage. But I do not wish to review only past accomplishments.
The C.B.C. has been frequently mentioned in this chamber in recent days and it would be well for us to remember how and why the corporation was established. The reason it was not made a department of government, that it was not made directly

responsible to parliament is tied in with the fact that in a country so large and thinly populated it would be difficult initially for private radio and television to produce the type of programs that all Canadians might well expect to see, and to do this at a financial profit. As a consequence there was a necessity for government ownership, and the objective was to have government ownership without government or parliamentary interference. Thus the C.B.C. was set up with a president and a board of 11 directors appointed from all across the country.
In 1958 the Broadcasting Act, repealing the Canadian broadcasting act, provided for the establishment of a board of broadcast governors, whose purpose was the provision "of a varied and comprehensive broadcasting service of a high standard. . . ." and which had the power to make regulations "respecting standards of programs." Regardless of what the B.B.G. has or has not done with this power, it must be remembered that the previous government gave the B.B.G. the power to make regulations regarding standards of programs, and it was the previous government which appointed the first members of the B.B.G.
Over the years frequent attempts have been made to interfere with the independence of the C.B.C., and in dealing with them the proper view has been that which was expressed so well by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings in 1962, when he held the cabinet portfolio which embraced the C.B.C. As recorded at page 857 of Hansard for February 14, 1962 he said:
-it has been the policy of this government from the beginning, as it was the policy of the previous government and as I hope it will always be the policy of federal governments, not to interfere

I am sure we all agree with the stand which he took on that occasion, but I hasten to say that I disagree with some of the things that are done by the C.B.C., and in particular I refer to certain programs that may be held to be in bad taste. I shall not again take the opportunity to criticize the C.B.C. in this chamber because I do not think this is the proper place to do it, but since we are on the subject I think we should be most concerned about the showing of a film that is highly controversial in the United States just prior to the eve of the presidential elections. I am sure there would be great

yelling and screaming on this side of the border if the Americans were to use their television facilities which come into this country, as ours go into parts of the United States, to put on controversial political material on the eve of a Canadian election.

Despite the fact that sometimes we all disagree with the policies of the C.B.C. we are in such a situation that were we to interfere with the policies of that corporation we could destroy its independence. At the present time an advisory committee is at work under Mr. Fowler, a committee made up of experts, looking into the development of the industry as a whole. Its report will be ready in the spring and would make an appropriate subject for consideration by a parliamentary committee. We would then have the opportunity to consider the report of this departmental committee and express the views of Canadians as their elected representatives. I think the meeting of a parliamentary committee now would be premature and without direction. I believe it would be used by many of the members of this house to indulge in program reviews, as they do periodically, reviews upon which they waste the time of the people here in the House of Commons. When this report comes before a parliamentary committee-and we have been told that such a committee will be set up next year-I believe it would be a good idea to have the officials come before us, in order that the general trend might be considered. But to hold meetings now would merely provide a platform for those in this house who want parliament to run the C.B.C. on a day by day basis. I would point out, also, that not only is it very late in the session but that we have a very heavy backload of business to attend to without taking on this extra responsibility now.
I wonder, however, whether the members who have spoken on this subject are really concerned at all about the general policies of the C.B.C. I think it more likely they are merely trying to establish a forum for their program reviews. Let us consider some of the things which have been said today. The hon. member for Edmonton West was very careful, when he spoke, to tell the committee he did not want to carry on a witch hunt or interfere with the independence of the corporation. But he did want to know, he said,

I do not hesitate to speak, nor do I apologize to anyone in this house for standing in my place saying those things I believe to be accurate about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and whether in my opinion it is doing a good or bad job. I am not afraid of any kind of retaliation. Everyone suggests that if you comment about the expenditures of a crown corporation you are engaging in a witch hunt. If by registering objections to pornography and perversion I am witch hunting, I say then, let us get on with this witch hunt. There are those who believe that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has for some time been the darling of the Liberal party, and that it is dedicated not only to the spreading of pornography and perversion, but also Liberalism. Mr. Chairman, I am not alone in my comments about the C.B.C. In Its general preamble, attached to a petition form, declaration states that both radio and t.v. are being exploited to maintain a constant assault on character, to undermine faith in God and

I want to speak a moment about programming. Last night I saw the program "This Hour Has Seven Days". I have a right to say what I think about it and I intend to do so. I am not ashamed of giving my opinion. Too many members of parliament look at crown corporations and expenditures on them and say: Our role is to say nothing; we must not say anything because we will take their freedom away from them.
I saw the program last night and I say it was in the worst traditions of third rate college high jinks. What was not in that spirit and taste was an outright and open attempt to whitewash certain people in the United States, particularly Walter Jenkins, the presidential aide. I was disgusted with the freedom that the C.B.C. gave the producers of the program to equate perversion of a homosexual nature with overzealousness in the public service. This is something I cannot accept. I was not amused, enlightened or even entertained by Mr. Rockwell, and the press reports of the reactions of great many Canadian people indicate that I am not alone in that view.
The sad part of all this in my opinion is that there is ample scope for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, with regard to whatever activities it wants to pursue, in keeping with its original mandate. Its mandate is by no means fulfilled and there is ample evidence that the corporation could come to parliament and secure appropriations of $80 million, $90 million or $100 million a year if it would carry out a positive program such as has yet to be enunciated. In other words, let the corporation get away from this nonsense of portraying perversion as though there were some kind of adolescent kick to it, and let it carry out the very necessary work that needs to be done.
I have some suggestions for the corporation. There are hundreds of thousands of Canadian people who are still without television service. There are thousands of Canadians who are not able to receive good radio broadcasts. I am thinking of the people who live in the northerly areas where the only station they can listen to is radio Moscow.

It is the only station that comes in consistently and it has good, impartial coverage of Canadian news.
These northerly areas are the areas of .greatest isolation and insulation and if there is anywhere in Canada where the educational and cultural possibilities of radio and television are desperately needed it is in these northern areas where the people are remote from the mainsprings of Canadian life. However, every time I ask the C.B.C. to look into these things I get the answer that the cost of extending these services would be too great.
This afternoon I made a telephone call to a C.B.C. officer to find out about their new building program. I learned that they are expecting to build two new office buildings in Toronto and Montreal. The one in Toronto will cost $45 million, the one in Montreal will cost $60 million and together with a few smaller ones there will be a total expenditure of approximately $108 million. This is so that those who now plan C.B.C. programs can do so in more comfort. I am not so sure that producers of pornography should be allowed to hatch their perversions in air conditioned comfort at a time when hundreds of thousands of Canadians have yet to receive any kind of basic service. What else might the C.B.C. do instead of pursuing this bent they have today? I believe, and I believe this sincerely, that the programming of this agency, now that we are in 1964, requires a careful review. I do not believe that it would be necessary to limit this program review to parliament, although I would have no objection to parliamentarians being on such a committee. I believe a re-examination of this corporation is needed, and is needed now. I do not believe that a member of parliament getting up to register an objection to filth is destroying the independence of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. If in fact this kind of filth is being perpetrated on the Canadian people, then I want to know who else in this country is going to stand up and oppose this sort of thing if members of parliament, individually and collectively, do not do it?

This is the sort of Liberal sophistry I have no difficulty in answering. I suggested a two point program. I suggested, (a) eliminating the filth and garbage and, (b) those energies that are now being directed to perversion should be devoted to bringing good Canadian broadcasting to the people of this country.

I hope the committee will forgive me for changing the topic. I would love to join in the discussion of the C.B.C., but the points I would like to bring up are really out of context with the debate that has taken place. It seems to me the questions about the C.B.C. that are most pressing are its relationship to commercial policy and its whole relationship to the board of broadcast governors. I am very much bothered by the lame duck status of the present chairman of the board of broadcast governors in relation to broadcasting policy. It seems to me that this type of approach and query that could be handled by a broadcasting committee would be more important in setting broadcasting and radio direction than in considering the perversions and pornography raised by the hon. member for the Northwest Territories. He will forgive me if I say to the house and to him that I really believe in assessing what he said he, himself, would have to acknowledge, that he was drawing a little bit of a long bow. I do not see how any of us, no matter what our contact with the C.B.C. may be, can fail to admit-I have had the kind of letters of complaint that have been mentioned-that the C.B.C. does not continually put out perversion and pornography upon the air waves via either television or radio. I do not believe it does those of us who are really 
critical of the C.B.C. any good to exaggerate in that particular direction.
Now, Mr. Chairman, what I wanted to speak to was the debate we had on Friday afternoon in connection with a situation on Canadian National Railways known as the run-through problem. Today the Prime Minister made an announcement that he was acceding to the request of the president of Canadian National Railways to set up a commission of inquiry. It would be under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, section 55, subsection (3). The commissioner would have terms of reference that would enable him to examine the situation in connection with run-throughs, arising particularly out of the situation at Wainwright and Nakina. Everyone may have assumed that once the Prime Minister made this announcement, everything would be over. The fact of the matter is that at this stage of the evening the railroad workers, in the main, have still not reported for work across much of Canada. I wanted to bring out some of the reasons for their hesitation, and why some of them are bitter about the situation. This was a spontaneous outburst that developed on Sunday without any triggering, I can assure you, by any third party as the president of Canadian National seems to allege in his telegram to the Prime Minister. Those who developed this spontaneous outburst are somewhat bitter over the fact the government and the Canadian National have not made a couple of points sufficiently clear.
The first point is the whole question about discipline and the kind of disciplinary action that may be taken by the management against the men. The reason there is bitterness is that last night, just at the most inopportune time in view of what happened today, across the system the railway forced letters upon employees informing them that if they were not back to work at midnight they would be out of service, and maybe on a permanent basis.
This kind of threat, coming as it did on the eve of what was imagined by the government to be a settlement, has left a bitterness that requires a very clear statement from the government that it has had an assurance from the C.N.R. that there will be no retaliation. I have received wires and phone calls from Kamloops, Edmonton, Melville, and places all over the country stressing this particular point.
I know the area vice presidents of the C.N.R., among them Mr. Gander in Toronto, have sent out wires to all terminal points

stating that the men can have this assurance, but one of the most telling commentaries on the bitterness in C.N.R. labour relations over the last few years is the fact that the men are doubtful of this word. Therefore one of the things that has to follow on this particular tie-up is a recognition by the Minister of Labour and the C.N.R. of the fact that the trust and kind of mutual regard that should exist in good Canadian labour relations has largely disappeared between the C.N.R. and its men. I only hope that this particular incident will give impetus to the development of that kind of trust, and will draw some initiative from the government.
I was tempted to review, as did the Leader of the Opposition on motions today, the somewhat sorry performance of the government on this occasion. On Friday the government argued against urgency of debate on the issue, and the minister got up and indicated the government's responsibility was merely to let representations go to the C.N.R. I say to hon. members, don't let what happened in terms of the wire from the president of the C.N.R. and the wire of the Prime Minister, kid you. Somebody on the government side must have made some representations over the week end. I think it shameful that we were denied an urgent debate on the question of urgency, solely because the government and one of its ministers made an argument that there was not any urgency. The reason the minister thought there was no urgency was because he did not understand there was going to be a blow-up on this particular problem.
The second thing that is bothering the men who are out of service across the country at present is the whole question of the scope of the terms of reference that the commissioner of inquiry will have. I want to put on record that I, as someone interested in the case, accept the assurance of the Minister of Labour and of the Minister of Transport that these terms of reference will be broad enough so that the whole problem of run-throughs can be examined and some solutions recommended to it.
What the men have campaigned for on run-throughs is some way of bringing the problem under contract negotiation so that there cannot be unilateral decision, as was the case last Saturday midnight, when the C.N.R. introduced this particular one. I know the Minister of Labour may not be in a position to give this assurance when he has set up this commission of inquiry, but I want to get very clearly on the record that if something like that does not resolve out

of the situation, then the other kind of solutions had better be wonderful in their completeness, thoroughness and ability to satisfy the men.
The main factor in the development of all this bitterness was the fact that the men were never able to negotiate this major change in their working conditions affecting their homes and families. It has always been at the initiative of management who could say, "Whether you like it or not, no matter what little adjustments we are prepared to make, the change is going to be made."
Even as late as yesterday the management of C.N.R. was trying to insist there would be no kind of agreement of any kind unless the men on the local levels were prepared to accept the recommendation that within two years the home divisional point at Nakina would be abolished.
There is one other point in connection with this matter that should be met. On Friday the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre brought up, as did I, the question of the 1926 Montreal agreement. I have seen copies of this agreement over the week end. It is one of the matters I know will be brought before the commissioner, and I want to put a particular section of it on the record so that the Minister of Labour and the government will realize just how much worth and value there is in it.
In May 1926 the brotherhood of locomotive firemen and enginemen and the brotherhood of locomotive engineers entered into an agreement with the C.N.R. This agreement was to last until it was rescinded after 30 days notice on the part of the management, and the point that is particularly important in connection with this document is that it has never been abrogated in any way. The company has never approached the unions with the suggestion that it be thrown out, and I want to point to one of the sections of the agreement which it seems to me is fundamental in a situation where a home terminal is being wiped out. Section 9 says:
Nothing in this agreement shall be taken to permit the company without prior conference with representatives of the employees to change existing home terminal stations of the employees affected thereby-
And it goes on to say that this will not apply when new facilities are created somewhere in the same city or community; but that part is irrelevant. Is there anything more clear so far as home terminals are concerned? This is one of the reasons why the men have felt all along that they have a justifiable

Interim Supply
grievance in the Nakina and Wainwright situation. This agreement and the schedule attached to it has been overlooked and completely ignored by the C.N.R. management.
There is one other point that I think the Minister of Labour should make clear to us. It is something the railroaders have been asking him for some time. They also asked it of his predecessor, the hon. member for Ontario, namely whether there could not be an amendment to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act so that they would have the opportunity of negotiating this kind of situation under that act; in other words, that any time there was a major change in their working conditions this would enable them to negotiate.
At present they do not have this protection under the act. As a matter of fact every time they have tried to enter into negotiations or objected to the changes, the company has always produced the threat contained in that section of the Criminal Code which requires them to honour the obligations they have entered into under their contract. This is the kind of assurance that would be fundamental and I would appreciate it if the Minister of Labour could make some comment on it.
Another point on which he or the Minister of Transport should speak concerns section 182 of the Railway Act which, if it was interpreted the way most of us think it should have been by the courts, or if it had been amended the way a parliamentary committee recommended last session, would give the railroaders and the communities concerned the protection they have been seeking.
The thing that I am proudest of in connection with this whole issue and the way it developed is the fact that the railroaders on the C.N.R. proved they are not mice, that they are not rabbits, as a lot of people thought. They came out in a magnificent display of the kind of solidarity which only comes when men are desperate. What I appreciate most about it was not that they thumbed the nose at the man who heads the C.N.R.- a man for whom I have not a great deal of respect-but what I am most appreciative of is the spirit shown by this little town in my constituency, a town which governments and railway managements tend to forget. These people persisted, though they had the devil of a time making their representations and getting them understood. And when the facts of the situation went down the wire on Saturday night, all I knew and all I could report was that the government would

not take any action and that from this point of view, the situation was dead.
I should like to remind hon. members that these people are living hundreds of miles from any large city and that their means of communication are very scant. It is not like a metropolitan community where it is possible to get legal advice and all kinds of assistance from a host of politicans, agencies and authorities. They are very much out on a limb. But when the moment came, they moved. They made a response and withdrew their services. And up and down the whole system the reply went along; Nakina and Wainwright were supported from Vancouver right through the piece. I appreciate this. I have to express this kind of appreciation because these constituents of mine are now convinced that even though the government did not show a great concern for them, their fellow workers across the whole system did, and I think this brewing up of a spirit of consideration among fellow railwaymen in different parts of the country is the most significant thing which has happened in labour relations and on the railroads for some time. I believe it will be a long time before railway management considers it can push through changes of the kind attempted last Saturday unilaterally and at such short notice.
I should like, too, to express my appreciation to the ladies of the town of Nakina who were out on the platform for trains at three, four, and five in the morning with posters, handing out leaflets, convincing the passengers and crews, shaming the officials who were running the trains yesterday to try to make them see that in a sense they were helping to kill, or lead to the death of, the community of Nakina.
I should like also to mention one of the ironies I spotted during these developments. More than four years ago a group of railwaymen came down from Capreol, Horne-payne and similar places. They saw the minister of labour and got nowhere with their representations against the company bringing in run-throughs. The unions leadership said they could do nothing for them. They came to me and asked me what I would suggest. I said that if they believed in their cause strongly enough they should be prepared to go to jail for it. I said that if they were prepared to do that they would be prepared to withdraw their services. I was hectored and bullied about this later on in the parliamentary committee before which the president of the C.N.R. appeared. But there was

one man who rose to this. He lit a Are and declared there was to be a wildcat strike. He was a man by the name of Shortt. He was the one who got a story to the newspapers, and the C.N.R. changed its mind very shortly-within a day or so. This man was promoted soon after; he became an official. And on Saturday night, in identically the same situation, he was the official who was taking the lead up in that area to make the run-through possible for management. I think this was one of the ironies, that promotion of someone who had been so vigorous on behalf of the men could lead to a situation in which this same man ran through nearly five divisions in some 18 hours pulling trains for management.
The last point I want to touch on in connection with this situation is the way in which the C.N.R. used its officials. One of the contentions some of us have made with regard to the C.N.R. is that there are too many chiefs in comparison with the number of Indians. Well, the C.N.R. had officials scattered right across the country yesterday running trains. I want to know more about this because it is my belief that if the company has all these superfluous officials who know how to run trains so as to be able to cover up when trains are tied up all across the country it does, indeed, have too many chiefs. Obviously if they could trim some of the chiefs they would worry less about a few of the Indians at some of the smaller places.
The Minister of Labour has been very good in this situation, particularly today, and I should like to express my appreciation to him and to his officials. I hope he will be able to bring forward terms of reference broad enough to do the job, and that he will be able to help create the kind of atmosphere between union and management which will establish trust-because trust has diminished, and diminished very severely, on the Canadian National Railways.

I was naturally surprised to hear the exaggerated statements made from both sides of the house. One side said that the C.B.C. was a den of corruption; the other, that it was a sacrosanct temple. One must nevertheless admit that both sides are exaggerating.
In my opinion, the C.B.C. is at present suffering from a growth problem which is normal in any modern enterprise. Television

came to Canada some 15 years ago. Therefore, the technical field, the studios and the reception centres had to be developed, and today ever increasing attention is paid to the production of programs.
In view of the fact that radio and television must face competition which is getting stronger and stronger, the C.B.C. feels it necessary to revitalize its ideas, and that is normal. You cannot broadcast programs 12, 15 and 16 hours a day during 10 or 15 years without trying something new, because obviously if you do not do so, people will be dissatisfied and will quit watching television. In this effort of renewal, errors may have been committed and not only within the C.B.C. but everywhere else. We must understand that.
It is obvious that there have been tasteless programs. In my opinion, it was not mainly due to a lack of taste but because in certain fields untalented persons have been launched in such a considerable undertaking. This is when we witnessed unsuccessful programs.
However, we must not blame the C.B.C. as a whole, because when we consider artistic programs, on the French network at least, everyone will agree, I am sure, that in the province of Quebec the C.B.C. introduced some very talented artists whom we had never heard before.
After all, musicians of great talent and real ability have been made known, thanks to the C.B.C. both on radio and on television, and now they tour the province, the country and even foreign countries giving recitals.
There are playwrights and composers who were able to make themselves known throughout the country thanks to the C.B.C., on either the French or the English network.
After all, there have been amateur sport programs which helped our young people and opened new horizons for them.
Of course mistakes have been made, but it must also be recognized that everything was not bad in the C.B.C. There were also successful programs. At least, we should be proud of the success achieved by C.B.C. in contributing to the bringing into notice of our Canadian authors, actors, artists, musicians, athletes, etc.
Errors were made and I think that there were so many protests across the country that the C.B.C. must have known about it then, as well as it knows now, after the discussion in this house today.
When we ask for the setting up of a committee whose members could deal with C.B.C.

management, we are not asking to administer the corporation as suggested by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Regan) a while ago. No, but we believe that such a meeting would be tremendously important and interesting both for the C.B.C. management and the hon. members. The C.B.C. is after all a government agency, and I agree that its directors must enjoy some independence as regards programming.
A short while ago the C.B.C. was compared with a business firm. Since the shareholders of a company meet the directors at least once a year and tell them what they think of their policies, I think that it should be the same with the C.B.C. whose operations cost the Canadian taxpayers between $80 and $85 million a year.
But the taxpayers' representatives have not even the opportunity of telling, once in a while, the officials of that crown corporation what the Canadian people think of them, while they can do it in the case of the C.N.R. As a matter of fact, we know that it had to be done, fortunately, with the administration of the C.N.R. in order that changes which we have noticed lately be made.
It was fortunate that hon. members could meet the president of Air Canada to tell him what they thought of Air Canada's service, for today we can see that its officials improved certain things. C.N.R. officials have also improved certain things.
The president of the C.N.R. may have found it hard during the few days he was a witness before the railways, canals and telegraph lines committee. The same thing can be said about the president of Air Canada, but at least they heard what the representatives of the people thought about those crown corporations and what changes they wanted made.
The presidents of those two crown corporations thought it advisable to take the members' representations into account, and even if changes were not made too quickly, at least some were made and the service was improved.
Why should we not be afforded the same opportunity to tell the C.B.C. officials what we think not only of the C.B.C.'s administration, but its programming, while not interfering with their independence, their freedom, in short, giving them, as before, a free hand in the administration of that agency?
Such an exchange of views would not be useless. In the past, it proved useful in the case of other crown corporations.
Political programs have been mentioned. In my opinion, hon. members, even those who

sit on the government side, would have some rather bitter remarks to make in certain cases to certain C.B.C. officials concerning the anarchy and violence they helped spread for a while. Indeed, Liberal members were the first to complain about that.
Would it not be useful to bring some examples and concrete facts to the attention of C.B.C. directors and officers?
Even if a director is competent it does not mean that he is an authority in all fields such as programming.
Maybe the president is a good accountant- though I doubt it in view of his deficit of $85 million-but even if he is a good businessman, that does not mean that he has the ability to judge the character and atmosphere of poitical programs, cultural programs or the general programming.

I shall try to speak more slowly, Mr. Chairman, to make it easier for the hon. member to understand, but after the arguments advanced a while ago by the hon. member for Halifax in his speech, I think that this will be hard.
In any event, such a meeting would be beneficial to everyone because, among other things, in the field of so-called political programs, they will have to admit that for some time now, the C.B.C. has been going astray and that there are in the service responsible for political programs individuals who are more interested in promoting certain ideas than putting forward ideas representing the average opinion of the Canadian people.
There are individuals-and this may be quite human-in the C.B.C., a crown corporation, who are only too anxious to please the party in office. Knowingly or unknowingly- and probably knowingly rather than unknowingly-they try to direct these programs according to a given policy rather than leave the corporation really independent, as some Liberal members were saying a while ago.
But, Mr. Chairman, over and above the C.B.C., there is today a more important problem in Canada. I refer to the economic situation prevailing in this country.
The Minister of Finance may tell us that Canada is prosperous because it has a surplus of $395 million but that is not a sign of prosperity; it means that taxes have increased and that more money has been taken from the taxpayers and the Canadian corporations.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) may tell us that unemployment is decreasing. Why? Because his statistics are inaccurate.

The Minister of Finance counts as jobless only those in receipt of unemployment insurance benefits, when there are others who do not work and are in receipt of social insurance; those people are also unemployed.
Unemployment did not decrease, it even increased. Statistics were falsified, altered.

Montreal, October 26, 1964
Various representations have been passed on to me by the Acting Minister of Transport with reference to the timing of the implementation of Canadian National operational plans for running through Nakina and Wainright. As the record shows we have made offers to purchase residences of employees who may move their homes from Nakina and have also undertaken moving expenses involved. Moreover at all times we have expressed willingness to very implementation timing or postpone inaugurations subject only to completion within two years.
We fully believe our discussions with employees affected and their union representatives would have reached amicable understandings as has been the case elsewhere and that present situation is due largely to intervention by third parties which has led to misunderstandings and distortions of actual situation.
We now wish to advise that if government is willing to appoint an independent and impartial person to examine into reasonableness of our proposals and plans for implementation Canadian National will withdraw run-through plans which were effective Sunday October 25 and withhold further action until report is made. We must assume of course that report can be made within reasonable period and respectfully suggest that three months should be ample. Will you please let me know if government is willing to give this assistance.

Ottawa, October 26, 1964
I very much welcome the suggestion in your telegram. On the understanding that you will withdraw run-through plans and withhold further action, the government is moving at once to appoint an independent and impartial person to undertake the examination you refer to. In view of the deterioration in the railway situation I am announcing your proposal and the government's action immediately.
